framework.name: People and Peace
framework.description:
This first Strategic Priority “People and Peace” of the UNSDCF addresses how the UN can support Kenya in its work to reduce its deep inequalities and lift all at risk of being left behind (particularly all women and girls; all youth and children; all in the Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASAL counties);  and all in the informal urban settlements) out of poverty and ensure their equitable access to quality services within a peaceful and well-governed society. 

Prioritizing People and Sustaining Peace: Addressing human capital development to achieve a peaceful and inclusive Kenyan society for sustainable development with access to justice for all and with effective, accountable and inclusive institutions at all levels is a top priority in Kenya’s development agenda: this is clearly stipulated in the Political and Social Pillars of “Kenya Vision 2030”. In this SP UN Kenya will focus on approaches and mechanisms to support strengthening of institutional capacities to implement laws and policies that promote human rights, human security, gender equality, access to justice, transparency, accountability and rule of law, in line with the Constitution and in compliance with regional and international commitments. 
This work will also focus on enhancing human capital and capacities at all levels of the government (including particularly at the level of the devolved county governments), non-state institutions and broader society and communities to efficiently deliver stigma-free, equitable, accessible, quality, and responsive, comprehensive services. The SP will address SDGs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 and 16. All of these are supported and underpinned by a strong focus on partnerships, SDG 17.

children.name: Outcome 1.1: By 2026, people in Kenya at risk of being left behind – particularly all women and girls, all children and youth, all people in the ASAL counties and in informal urban settlements – inhabit an inclusive, enabling, socially cohesive, and peaceful society where human rights are upheld, and benefit from accountable institutions and participate in transformative governance systems that are gender responsive and uphold the rule of law.
children.description:
Despite strong progress in enhancing the rule of law, human-rights, gender equality and cohesion, obdurate obstacles require attention. These include inter-ethnic competition, corruption and structural inequalities. UN Kenya will support the Government to develop approaches and mechanisms to support institutional strengthening and build capacities to formulate, review and implement laws, policies and budgeting frameworks that promote peace and cohesion, human rights, human security, gender equality, access to justice, transparency, accountability and rule of law, in line with the Constitution and in compliance with regional and international commitments. 
Specific support includes:
•	Enhanced institutional and human capacities at national and devolved level to implement laws and policies that are inclusive, responsive and promote human rights, peace, human security, gender equality, access to justice, transparency, accountability, and rule of law, in line with the Constitution and in compliance with regional and international commitments with a particular focus on children and youth, women and girls, people living in the ASALs and in urban informal settlements. 
•	Strengthened devolution and inter-governmental relations to enhance coordination for inclusive, equitable, transparent, accountable, and effective service delivery for all citizens including women, youth, children and those at risk of being left behind particularly in the ASALs and in urban informal settlements.
Among actions that UN Kenya intends to launch with the GoK and county governments under the UNSDCF, a serious focus on policies and resources to enhance devolution and address inequalities will be central. So will concrete and consistent support from the UN to ensure robust planning frameworks linked to the SDGs in all sectors. A number of powerful joint programmes are envisioned under this outcome. These could include a joint programme on peace and security, one on migration, mobility and regional integration and one joint programme on access to justice, human rights and rule of law. And finally, a joint programme on self-reliance for refugees and host communities benefitting both refugees and hosting communities in ASAL areas is envisioned, with inclusive programming to support the Government’s expressed intention to transform Kenya’s longstanding and generous hosting of refugee populations in camps to integrated settlements, in line with the Global Compact on Refugees.

children.name: Outcome 1.2: By 2026, people in Kenya at risk of being left – particularly all women and girls, all children and youth, all people in the ASAL counties and in informal urban settlements – have improved, inclusive and equitable social and protection services.
children.description:
Kenya’s social service and social protection safety net are growing admirably in scope and scale. But they remain sub-optimal because of a lack coherence across the three pillars: social assistance, social security and health insurance. This, in turn, stems from both a lack of overarching legislation and inadequate funding. Also, despite a decline in adult HIV prevalence, social, legal and policy challenges continue to impede effective response to HIV, amongst them, stigma and discrimination, access to justice and gender inequality. 
UN Kenya will support the Government to address these challenges by enhancing capacities of national and county government, non-state institutions and communities to efficiently deliver stigma-free, equitable, accessible, quality, and responsive services. The capacity of government will also be enhanced to deliver integrated sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health services, leaving no one behind, including vulnerable and marginalised populations. 
Specific support include:
•	Enhanced systems and capacity of the national and county governments, non-state institutions and communities to efficiently deliver inclusive, accessible and equitable health (including RMNCAH), HIV, WASH and Food and Nutrition services to women and girls, children and youth – particularly in the ASALs and in informal urban settlements.
•	Enhanced systems and capacity of the national and county governments, non-state institutions and communities to efficiently deliver inclusive, accessible, equitable, resilient education, child protection, migration, social protection, GBV and FGM services to women and girls, children and youth – particularly in the ASALs and in informal urban settlements.
Here the UNSDCF identifies among other things the importance of a strategic push to complete universal health coverage, and – in keeping with the LNOB lens – special attention to access to WASH and nutrition in the ASALs. Under outcome 1.2 a wide range of joint programmes are envisioned: starting with the existing HIV joint programme; one joint programme on adolescence, sexual and reproductive health; one joint programme on anti-microbial resistance encompassing both animal and human health sectors; one joint programme to combat gender-based violence through a cross sectoral approach; a social services, migration services and social protection joint programme; and finally a joint programme on youth, including technical and vocational education and training and job creation, building on the successes of the Government-led “Generation Unlimited” initiative.

framework.name: "Prosperity and planet"
framework.description:
The second Strategic Priority ”Prosperity and Planet” focuses on how the UN can support the Kenyan economy to become an early and successful adapter to the Green Transition, including all at risk of being left behind (particularly all women and girls; all youth and children; all in the ASAL counties;  and all in the informal urban settlements) while preserving ecosystem services restored and intact.


The importance of conserving biodiversity, advancing a “green transition” and combatting and adapting to the impact of the climate emergency are all centrally articulated in the Government of Kenya’s development policies and strategies – especially in both the Economic and Social Pillars of “Kenya Vision 2030”. The Government intends to incorporate best practices in climate change mitigation and adaptation and promoting an inclusive green economy through the new MTP IV, while continuing to fast-track implementation of the SDGs and the goals of AU Agenda 2063. The Central Bank of Kenya has also issued guidance for the financial sector on climate-related risk management and the Governor of the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) also announced early 2022 that “Kenya should become a premier green finance hub”.

Kenya aspires to be a global leader on environment and innovation and has an ambition to transform the value chains of nature-based enterprises including in agriculture, nutrition and food/livelihood security, and affordable and clean energy. Our recent UN CCA identified massive opportunity for Kenya to accelerate its green transition, which is challenged by biodiversity loss and failing ecosystems services. Under this SP, the UN will focus on addressing environmental and climatic challenges and to shift the Kenyan economy to a green trajectory by supporting the Government to increase opportunities for green and sustainable investments and enhance enabling environment to achieve quality livelihoods and decent work for those furthest behind, particularly the youth, women, people in the ASALs and urban informal settlements, while ensuring sustainably managed ecosystems for nature-based solutions in a green transition. This SP addresses SDG 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 together with 13, 14 and 15. All of these are supported and underpinned by a strong focus on partnerships, SDG 17.

children.name: Outcome 2.1: By 2026, people in Kenya at risk of being left behind – particularly all women and girls, all children and youth, all people in the ASAL counties and in informal urban settlements – derive benefit from inclusive, sustainable, diversified and environmentally/climate-sensitive quality livelihoods with decent work in the sector economies and realize growth that is resilient, green, and equitable
children.description:
Kenya’s natural resources (its flora and fauna, its land, its water courses and lakes and its forests) are extraordinary. But these are at risk of continued degradation, due to the climate emergency, unregulated human activities and unsustainable agricultural practices that have led to low production and soil losses. There is increasing ecosystem degradation in the upstream water catchment areas and wetlands, affecting availability of safe drinking water and sanitation services. These challenges have negatively impacted on people’s livelihoods and reduced opportunities for decent work. The very same has enhanced climate emergency effects leading Kenya to also suffer from cyclical climate related disasters, pest and disease outbreak, often resulting in resource-based conflicts. But on the positive side of the balance sheet, Kenya is already close to achieving sustainable energy self-sufficiency, with great economic prospects of becoming a major exporter of sustainable energy in the wider region. And there is enormous wider potential to sustainably develop the green and blue economy for economic progression and livelihoods to stem inequality and improve socio-economic conditions while progressively regenerating critical ecosystems.
The UN will address environmental and climate challenges and their related disaster impact by supporting the Government to promote multi-dimensional resilience. UN Kenya will also support increased opportunities for investments in the green and blue economies and enhancing an enabling environment to achieve quality livelihoods and with decent work with particular focus on youth, women, PWD, PWHIV, people in the ASALs and in urban informal settlements. In addition, the UN will also seek to build technical development and capacities of MSMEs while also enhance sustainable urbanisation. Specific support includes:
•	Increased inclusive and sustainable green and blue production, investments and technologies (including digital) in the productive, service sectors and sustainable consumption to create resilient livelihoods for the benefit of youth, women, PWDs, people in ASALs and in urban informal settlements
•	 Strengthened capacities and policies/strategies of institutions and communities for climate action, disaster risk management and justice for the benefit of youth, women, PWDs, people in ASALs and urban informal settlements
To just mention a few examples, UN Kenya together with stakeholders aim to support the green transition of the Kenyan economy through support to the continued development of sustainable blue and green economies and job creation, but also to innovative climate-smart livelihoods and housing. Here UN Kenya envisions a broad joint programme on sustainable investment, consumption, and production in green and blue economy at county and community level. This would entail enabling and adequately resourced policy frameworks, gender responsive innovative technology, climate smart livelihoods, technical and business development capacities, decent jobs, research and development, sustainable county and community level engagement that would encompass empowering policies. Community-based climate adaptation and multi-dimensional resilience will also be a focus. UN Kenya sees the potential to drive a flagship joint programme on disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation that would strengthen multidimensional resilience (both economic and nature shocks) and adaptive capacity of communities to disasters and emergencies including from climate change.

Biodiversity loss due to climate and negative human activities has negatively impacted the socio-economic development of Kenya and it will have even larger negative consequences in the future. Key to this will be to restore ecosystems to derive benefit for people most at risk of being left behind. Specific support includes:
•	Terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems restored, protected and sustainably managed for the benefit of youth, women, PWDs, people in ASALs and urban informal settlements.
UN sees the potential to drive a joint programme on restoration and protection of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems. Elements for such joint action for nature-based solutions and restored ecosystems include support to the policy and legal frameworks with adequate resources for implementation and also capacity by counties and national level to access available climate and green finance. Partnership for Outcomes 2.1 and 2.2 – These two outcomes focus on economic development through the green transition and nature preservation and conservation respectively and the success of each is dependent on the other. A sustainable environment is a prerequisite for a green and sustainable economic growth and vice versa. Equally, the partners that work need to come together more closely and make sure that initiatives taken for green economic growth are done while remaining within the planetary boundaries preserving or restoring eco systems services. The UN will work with a wide and crosscutting range of stakeholders and partners including the Government to support delivery of the outcome including but not limited to: Government Ministries and departments (eg. Environment, Agriculture, Industrialisation, Labour, ASALs), NDMA, NEMA, COG, County governments, FCDC, Development Partners (Multilateral & bilateral), World Bank, International Monetary Fund, Kenya Red Cross Society, CSOs and particularly the private sector.

framework.name: Partnerships
framework.description:
The two first Strategic Priorities are underpinned by a Strategic Enabler on ”Partnerships” to support Kenya’s work to innovate and maximize the potential of multi-stakeholder partnerships, aligning available financial resources (domestic & international, public & private) to the attainment of the SDGs.

Since Kenya emerged as a lower middle-income country in September 2014, traditional ODA has been declining. This tendency is unlikely to reverse – indeed, it has recently been accelerating, due to the fiscal pressures exerted on traditional donor partners by COVID-19 and the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, the fiscal situation in Kenya is under pressure, occasioned by declining tax revenues and debt obligations that consume almost a third of budgetary space. This has been exacerbated by the same external factors: the COVID-19 pandemic (which occasioned national borrowing) and the war in Ukraine (which has already seen heightened commodity and fuel prices), as well recurrent drought emergencies. 
Thus, both domestic and international public resources for development are constrained. To deliver the SDGs and Vision 2030, Kenya therefore recognizes the centrality of building and deepening effective multi-stakeholder partnerships to mobilize the necessary human and capital resources at scale. Under the UNSDCF, UN Kenya will foreground an intense focus on strengthening multi-stakeholder partnerships to drive a much greater amount and diversity of public, private and community collaboration and financing to achieve the SDGs at the national and county levels. UN Kenya will play a vital role of curating and connecting and creating a conducive investment landscape for investments in the SDGs. The Strategic Enabler addresses mainly SDGs 17 although partnerships and collaboration compliments and supports all SDGs implementation. In principle under this new UNSDCF, UN Kenya’s intention is to routine a simple reflection with respect to any new programme to be launched: is there a clear and obvious role for multi-stakeholder partnership – particularly with the private sector – to drive this initiative to scale?

children.name: Outcome 3.1: By 2026, Kenya’s path to achieving SDGs benefits from effective multiple stakeholder partnerships to drive a greater amount and diversity of public, private and community collaboration as well as financing and investments that accelerate sustainable development for people in Kenya at risk of being left behind – particularly all women and girls, all children and youth, all people in the ASAL counties and in informal urban settlements.
children.description:
Kenya has experienced a significant reduction in Official Development Assistance (ODA) since the rebasing of the economy in September 2014 and the subsequent graduation to a lower middle-income (LMIC) country. This transition resulted in reduced UN and bilateral grants and led to increased government borrowing of expensive commercial loans. The ODA shortfall necessitated the diversification of financing streams to support national development priorities and achieve Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

In addition to the ODA challenges, Kenya has faced a decline in Foreign Direct Investments (FDIs), which has further constrained the availability of development financing. Compounding this, the government has encountered persistent difficulties in raising revenues above 20% of GDP, limiting its fiscal capacity to address critical developmental needs.

To address these challenges, the United Nations is supporting the Government of Kenya to strengthen multi-stakeholder partnerships. These partnerships aim to drive greater amounts and diversity of public, private, and community collaboration, ensuring progress toward the realization of SDGs at both national and county levels. Additionally, the UN is enhancing the availability and accessibility of evidence to inform development planning, budgeting, monitoring, and evaluation processes, empowering policymakers with robust data to optimize resource allocation and achieve impactful outcomes.

Our Strategic Enabler on Partnerships has a single outcome and is intended to serve as “force multiplier” for the four outcomes under SP1 and SP2. It is here that UN Kenya will concentrate on sharpening our work to build innovative partnerships and identify private sector actors who can capitalise on business opportunities for the SDGs, as part of the vital shift “from funding to financing”. We intend to help build the vital necessary bridge between the private sector and its wish to identify new market opportunities on the one hand and the realm of development and realisation of the SDGs on the other, where these new investment opportunities arise in need for investors. This strategic enabler will also be the locus of our work on data for development. UN Kenya will seek joint funding and financing mechanisms to underpin the UNSDCF and will primarily work through a set of large and impactful joint programmes and these will be funded through our new MPTF modality, “SDG MPTF Kenya”. The MPTF will work for all UN entities and will help minimise administrative burdens and transaction costs for Government and partners alike. projects.description:
A Development Impact Bond (DIB) is a results-based investment instrument that involves three parties: a private investor, an outcome payer, and an implementing partner/service provider. In practice, a DIB can have more than one of each type of partner. The private investor—usually a fund or group of investors—gives money to carry out a development programme that promises certain social outcomes. The service provider, usually a nonprofit organization, is responsible for the project and its outcomes. If the outcomes are achieved, the investor is paid back the capital plus interest by the outcome payer, usually a philanthropic funder or organization, upon verification by an independent evaluator.
The ASRH DIB in Kenya was launched in July 2023 with the aim of improving the sexual and reproductive health outcomes among adolescent girls (15-19 years) by enhancing access to quality adolescent and youth-friendly services among vulnerable adolescent girls and ultimately addressing the challenges of teenage pregnancy, new HIV infections, and AIDS-related deaths.

projects.description:
This Joint Programme (JP) aims to support Kenya’s transition to a circular and sustainable green and blue economy that is inclusive, gender-responsive, and climate-resilient. It focuses on transforming the country’s agri-food and blue economy systems—currently dominated by a wasteful linear model—into resource-efficient, regenerative models through nature-based solutions, innovative business practices, and ecosystem restoration.
The JP targets vulnerable groups including women, youth, and communities in ASALs and informal urban settlements, promoting sustainable investment, green jobs, and value chain development across key sectors such as fisheries, agriculture, textiles, and forestry. It is implemented in partnership with county governments, national ministries, civil society, and the private sector, and coordinated by FAO, UNIDO, UNEP, and UN Women. With a total budget of USD 36 million over four years (2024–2028), the JP contributes to Kenya’s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

projects.description:
The programme seeks to transform Kenya’s coffee sector into a catalytic driver of inclusive, green, and resilient economic development. Anchored in the principles of the 2030 Agenda and Kenya’s own development frameworks—such as Vision 2030, the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy (ASTGS)—this Joint Programme brings together multiple UN agencies, government actors, and private sector partners under a shared ambition: to unlock sustainable development through value chain transformation.
The programme is led by UNDP as the convening agency and implemented jointly with FAO, UN Women, UNIDO, and UNEP, in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development and county governments in key coffee-growing regions. It is supported through the UN SDG Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MPTF), with co-financing expected from public and private sources.
At its core, the programme aims to reposition the coffee value chain as a strategic lever for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially those related to poverty reduction, gender equality, decent work, responsible production, and climate action. It recognizes that despite its historical and economic significance, Kenya’s coffee sector has been constrained by policy bottlenecks, limited value addition, environmental degradation, and exclusion of women and youth.
To address these challenges, the programme is structured around three mutually reinforcing outcomes:
1.	An Enabling Policy and Investment Environment: The programme will support ongoing policy and regulatory reforms in the coffee sector to enhance transparency, attract investment, and promote quality standards. It will also establish a blended finance facility to de-risk private investment and develop bankable investment cases that align with SDG priorities.
2.	Sustainable Coffee Production and Climate Action: Farmers will be supported to adopt climate-smart, regenerative agricultural practices, including intercropping, agroforestry, and organic soil management. The programme will contribute to land restoration, improved soil health, and biodiversity protection while reducing emissions from agricultural practices. Eco-certification and climate adaptation will be central pillars of resilience building within farming communities.
3.	Inclusive Coffee Value Chain Development: The programme will focus on expanding market access through digital traceability systems, product differentiation, and branding of Kenyan coffee. Special emphasis will be placed on supporting women and youth to access opportunities in coffee production, processing, and entrepreneurship. Training, financial inclusion, and cooperatives will be leveraged to drive equitable participation and benefits.
By embedding environmental sustainability, gender responsiveness, and inclusive finance into all stages of the value chain, the programme seeks to create decent livelihoods, strengthen Kenya’s global positioning as a producer of premium, sustainable coffee, and contribute meaningfully to the SDGs. It reflects a systems approach that bridges climate action, economic empowerment, and sustainable trade.
In doing so, this initiative not only aligns with UNSDCF 2022–2026 Pillar II: Prosperity and Planet but also serves as a replicable model for how green value chains can unlock blended finance, deliver climate co-benefits, and enable locally led sustainable development.

projects.description:
This Joint Programme (JP) aims to support Kenya’s transition to a circular and sustainable green and blue economy that is inclusive, gender-responsive, and climate-resilient. It focuses on transforming the country’s agri-food and blue economy systems—currently dominated by a wasteful linear model—into resource-efficient, regenerative models through nature-based solutions, innovative business practices, and ecosystem restoration.
The JP targets vulnerable groups including women, youth, and communities in ASALs and informal urban settlements, promoting sustainable investment, green jobs, and value chain development across key sectors such as fisheries, agriculture, textiles, and forestry. It is implemented in partnership with county governments, national ministries, civil society, and the private sector, and coordinated by FAO, UNIDO, UNEP, and UN Women. With a total budget of USD 36 million over four years (2024–2028), the JP contributes to Kenya’s Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda and the UN Sustainable Development Cooperation Framework.

projects.description:
The programme seeks to transform Kenya’s coffee sector into a catalytic driver of inclusive, green, and resilient economic development. Anchored in the principles of the 2030 Agenda and Kenya’s own development frameworks—such as Vision 2030, the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy (ASTGS)—this Joint Programme brings together multiple UN agencies, government actors, and private sector partners under a shared ambition: to unlock sustainable development through value chain transformation.
The programme is led by UNDP as the convening agency and implemented jointly with FAO, UN Women, UNIDO, and UNEP, in partnership with the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development and county governments in key coffee-growing regions. It is supported through the UN SDG Multi-Partner Trust Fund (MPTF), with co-financing expected from public and private sources.
At its core, the programme aims to reposition the coffee value chain as a strategic lever for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially those related to poverty reduction, gender equality, decent work, responsible production, and climate action. It recognizes that despite its historical and economic significance, Kenya’s coffee sector has been constrained by policy bottlenecks, limited value addition, environmental degradation, and exclusion of women and youth.
To address these challenges, the programme is structured around three mutually reinforcing outcomes:
1.	An Enabling Policy and Investment Environment: The programme will support ongoing policy and regulatory reforms in the coffee sector to enhance transparency, attract investment, and promote quality standards. It will also establish a blended finance facility to de-risk private investment and develop bankable investment cases that align with SDG priorities.
2.	Sustainable Coffee Production and Climate Action: Farmers will be supported to adopt climate-smart, regenerative agricultural practices, including intercropping, agroforestry, and organic soil management. The programme will contribute to land restoration, improved soil health, and biodiversity protection while reducing emissions from agricultural practices. Eco-certification and climate adaptation will be central pillars of resilience building within farming communities.
3.	Inclusive Coffee Value Chain Development: The programme will focus on expanding market access through digital traceability systems, product differentiation, and branding of Kenyan coffee. Special emphasis will be placed on supporting women and youth to access opportunities in coffee production, processing, and entrepreneurship. Training, financial inclusion, and cooperatives will be leveraged to drive equitable participation and benefits.
By embedding environmental sustainability, gender responsiveness, and inclusive finance into all stages of the value chain, the programme seeks to create decent livelihoods, strengthen Kenya’s global positioning as a producer of premium, sustainable coffee, and contribute meaningfully to the SDGs. It reflects a systems approach that bridges climate action, economic empowerment, and sustainable trade.
In doing so, this initiative not only aligns with UNSDCF 2022–2026 Pillar II: Prosperity and Planet but also serves as a replicable model for how green value chains can unlock blended finance, deliver climate co-benefits, and enable locally led sustainable development.

projects.description:
The overall objective; Build the climate resilience of communities living in slums and informal settlements in Kenyan urban areas that are highly vulnerable to the impacts of climate change, primarily through gender
Transformative urban planning, green based economy livelihoods, and by putting communities at the center.
Specific objectives;
a)	To increase investment and financing to inclusive pro-poor and non-discriminatory adaptation projects in vulnerable hotspots’ in cities, informal settlements and communities where underlying socio-economic vulnerability are exacerbated by increased exposure to impact of climate change
b)	To strengthen capacity for the urban poor through holistic approaches including community-based adaptation of green economic livelihoods and tenure security

projects.description: WFP will promote readiness of National and County governments in Kenya to effectively anticipate, prepare for, manage and respond to emergencies with a climate lense. By supporting government to generate and use evidence from food and nutrition security assessments and earth observation to better prepare and respond faster to droughts and other climate-related shocks. Envisaged capacity strengthening areas include, on contingency planning, multi hazard early Warning system for Anticipatory Action and scaling up the reach of AAs with an activation. Others are supporting national and county institutions when it comes to adoption of new technologies, designing programmes and ensuring good service delivery to Kenya’s vulnerable populations (e.g., digital platforms such as supply chain management information systems, Kenya’s Relief Assistance Management Information System (RAMIS). In addition, at county level will be the support towards the set-up and strengthen the capacities of  Emergency Operation Centres (EOC) that are at the core of coordination and faster response in times of crises
